quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-01.title: Commuting direct factors
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-01.body:
Since $S,T\trianglelefteq G$ and $S\cap T=1$, $[S,T]\subseteq S\cap T=1$, so $S$ and $T$ commute elementwise.

**(a)** As $S\trianglelefteq G$, $S\cap H\trianglelefteq H$. Also $T$ centralizes $S\cap H\subseteq S$, so $T$ normalizes it. Hence $N_G(S\cap H)\supseteq HT=G$, i.e. $S\cap H\trianglelefteq G$. The argument for $T\cap H$ is symmetric (using $G=SH$).

**(b)** By the second isomorphism theorem, $G/S=SH/S\cong H/(S\cap H)\cong H$. Since $G=S\times T$, $G/S\cong T$. So $T\cong H$, and by symmetry $S\cong H$; hence $S\cong T$.

**(c)** With $H\trianglelefteq G$: $[H,S]\subseteq H\cap S=1$ and $[H,T]\subseteq H\cap T=1$. So $H$ centralizes $S$ and $T$. Then $C_G(S)\supseteq HT=G$ and $C_G(T)\supseteq HS=G$, so $S,T\subseteq Z(G)$ and $G=ST\subseteq Z(G)$: $G$ is abelian. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-03.title: Spanning sets and degree counting
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-03.body:
Let $F=\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$.

**(a)** Let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be a $K$-basis of $F_2$, $n=|F_2:K|$, and $L=\sum_kF_1a_k$. Each $a_ia_j\in F_2=\sum_kKa_k$, so $L$ is closed under multiplication; it is a subring of $E$ containing $F_1$ and $F_2$, an integral domain, and a finite-dimensional $F_1$-vector space. A finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is injective, hence surjective). So $L$ is a field containing $F_1,F_2$, contained in $F$; thus $L=F$, and $|F:F_1|\le n$ since $a_1,\dots,a_n$ span.

**(b)** By (a), $|F:K|=|F:F_1|\,|F_1:K|\le|F_2:K|\,|F_1:K|$. Both $|F_1:K|$ and $|F_2:K|$ divide $|F:K|$, and they are coprime, so their product divides $|F:K|$. Hence equality.

**(c)** $K=\mathbb{Q}$, $F_1=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $F_2=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ inside $E=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,i)$. Since $F_1\subset\mathbb{R}$, $i\notin F_1$, so $|F:F_1|=|F_1(i):F_1|=2$ and $|F:\mathbb{Q}|=4=2\cdot2$.

**(d)** $F/K$ is Galois (compositum of Galois extensions: splitting field of the product of the defining polynomials). Restriction gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)\to\mathrm{Gal}(F_1/K)\times\mathrm{Gal}(F_2/K)$; if $\sigma\in\ker\theta$, it fixes $F_1$ and $F_2$, hence $F$, so $\theta$ is injective. Orders: $|\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)|=|F:K|=|F_1:K||F_2:K|$, which is the order of the product. So $\theta$ is an isomorphism. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-04.title: Invariant kernels and images
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-04.body:
**(a)** Let $N=\ker A$. Clearly $AN=0\subseteq N$; and for $v\in N$, $A(Bv)=\lambda B(Av)=0$, so $BN\subseteq N$. Hence $N=0$ or $V$; $N=V$ means $A=0$, excluded. So $A$ is injective. Let $I=AV$. Then $AI\subseteq I$ and $B(Av)=\lambda^{-1}A(Bv)\in I$. So $I=0$ or $V$; $I=0$ means $A=0$. So $A$ is onto. Using $BA=\lambda^{-1}AB$, the same arguments show $\ker B$ and $BV$ are invariant under both, so $B$ is one-to-one and onto.

**(b)** Let $n=\dim V$ (finite, and $n\ge1$ since $A\ne0$). Taking determinants in $AB=\lambda BA$ gives $\det A\det B=\lambda^n\det B\det A$. By (a), $\det A,\det B\neq0$, so $\lambda^n=1$.

**(c)** On $V=\mathbb{C}^2$ let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=-BA$. A proper nonzero invariant subspace would be a line invariant under $A$, hence $\mathbb{C}e_1$ or $\mathbb{C}e_2$ (the eigenspaces of $A$, as its eigenvalues are distinct); but $B$ swaps $e_1$ and $e_2$. So no proper nonzero subspace is invariant under both. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-05.title: Direct computation
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2000f-05.body:
**(a)** $A_r(a+b)=(a+b)r-r(a+b)=A_r(a)+A_r(b)$, and
$$A_r(ab)=abr-rab=a(br-rb)+(ar-ra)b=aA_r(b)+A_r(a)b.$$

**(b)** Let $z\in Z$, $r\in R$. Applying $D$ to $rz=zr$:
$$rD(z)+D(r)z=D(rz)=D(zr)=zD(r)+D(z)r.$$
Since $z$ is central, $D(r)z=zD(r)$, leaving $rD(z)=D(z)r$. So $D(z)\in Z$.

**(c)** (Here $R$ has $1$, as in the hint.) By (b), $D(e)\in Z$, so $e$ and $D(e)$ commute, and
$$D(e)=D(e^2)=eD(e)+D(e)e=2eD(e).$$
Thus $(1-2e)D(e)=0$. Now $(1-2e)^2=1-4e+4e^2=1$, so multiplying on the left by $1-2e$ gives $D(e)=0$. ∎
